prospect.name: Rodrigo
prospect.location: Los Angeles, USA; calling from an apartment in Tulum, Mexico; returning to Los Angeles from 1 August for roughly three months
prospect.occupation: Creative producer for television; travels heavily for work; describes himself as a designer and technologist
prospect.training_background: Roughly twenty years of continuous self-directed training. Structures his year as three-to-twelve-month self-set challenges and has completed every one. Weights, calisthenics, yoga, running, cycling. Has followed Trevor for about a year and folds individual kettlebell movements into his own sessions. Trains at Planet Fitness at $28 a month.
prospect.medical: Permanent AC joint separation in one shoulder from an old injury — visible, not painful except when sleeping on that side. Bilateral tennis elbow: a severe episode two to three years ago that stopped him training entirely — 'I couldn't even hold a water bottle' — and which he says has never fully healed and is 'always there'. Right shoulder pain on chest work. Knee pinch on deep squats that eases after about five reps.

signals: Actively comparison-shopping four providers at once: 'I talked to three different companies, three different people that also they're waiting for my answer. So I'm just shopping around.'

Anchored to a genuinely working cheap alternative — twenty years of self-programming plus Planet Fitness at $28 a month — and says so plainly: 'Can I do it by myself? Absolutely, Richard. I can do it by myself. I've been doing it for 20 years.'
Weighs the purchase against lifestyle spend rather than against outcomes: 'for less than a thousand, I can sign up for this Tulum gym and the LA fitness, the gym that I want to go to, the spa level.'

Divergence from the archetype: he is affluent and explicitly says the value is there — 'if I didn't mind, I will pay 4,000 for that program. So I think it's totally worth it' — which is optimizer behaviour. He is shopping on rate of return, not on ability to pay.

goals.text: Get back to the physique he had three years ago — ripped, athletic, defined, Greek rather than bulky
Build muscle from within that stays on rather than deflating when he stops training
Learn kettlebell technique properly for the years to come rather than guessing at a technical movement
Have a new three-month challenge to follow so he does not get bored
Build a wide, strong chest, which he finds hardest to develop
Stop feeling the elbows, shoulder and knee during training
Have the best healthy body he can have as he ages

pains.text: Bilateral tennis elbow from a severe episode two to three years ago that never fully healed and is always present
Permanent AC joint separation leaving one arm stronger than the other and possibly loading the rest of his body unevenly
Right shoulder pain on chest work and a knee pinch on deep squats
Muscle he builds with weights deflates within three months of stopping — 'it's kind of like a balloon'
Gets bored very easily and needs constant novelty or he stops
Hard gainer; has to eat heavily and train constantly to hold muscle
Hates app-heavy programmes that take an hour of logging to get one answer
Cannot commit to six or twelve months of something he has not felt in his own body

objections.raw_quote: I don't, what I want to, what I don't want to do is like pay you six months. then at one month happened, I was like, I don't really like this. And I lost my money.
objections.rep_response: Probed whether he wanted a three-month lock or a one-month trial, then later quoted a three-month price of $4,000.

objections.raw_quote: that's the reason why I'm in a very cheap gym, like I'm in a Planet Fitness, $28 a month, and I'm happy, and I'm happy because that's the lifestyle of that gym
objections.rep_response: Asked whether joining a different gym would actually deliver the next level, then conceded 'if you're looking for a cheaper price, then he's definitely not the fit'.

objections.raw_quote: it's something that I need to, I didn't know that it was quite that amount
objections.rep_response: Justified with Trevor's experience — 'has worked with more than 1200 people' — and offered to reconvene the following day.

objections.raw_quote: I can think about this. I'm going to really dive mind-wise and then get back to you.
objections.rep_response: Proposed a call the next day: 'How about we jump on a call again tomorrow, just to hear your thoughts, and then if that all makes sense, we get you started tomorrow.'

objections.raw_quote: what I don't want is spend one hour in just loading how many grams of chicken I ate, so you tell me, and then I'm like, and then it starts feeling like, am I just doing this for my mindset, or they're actually seeing this
objections.rep_response: Deflected with a joke — 'getting on a call with us is indeed quite a bit of work, I know. After that, it's very simplicity' — then presented the filmed-workout and app-logging model unchanged.

evidence: No decision was reached: 'I'm just going to think, dive my brain into this with this knowledge, this information, and this amount, and see, okay, cool. I need to think if it's something that I wanted to commit to it.'
He committed to a concrete next step within the hour: 'I text you in the next hour, just to make sure... I can text you to your text, and I can tell you if it's tomorrow or maybe Friday.'
Rep committed to call if he does not hear back.

Counter-evidence: he announced an eight-minute hard stop before the offer was delivered and the rep chose to compress the whole presentation and price into it rather than rebook, despite having offered to rebook.
Counter-evidence: he is actively evaluating three competing programmes and has already rejected one of them for pushing too hard, so the sales style itself is under assessment.
outcome.next_step: Prospect to text within the hour to schedule a follow-up call for the next day or Friday. Rep to phone him if nothing arrives.

notable.note: Two things. First, the rep quoted a three-month tier at $4,000 that does not exist in the stated offer, and before that answered a direct price question with 'It's definitely the four figures' and 'around 1,000 a month, a little bit more, probably'. Second, the prospect objected to the app-logging and video-submission model before it was presented, the rep deflected with a joke, and then presented exactly that model. He also stated the value is there at $4,000 — 'if I didn't mind, I will pay 4,000 for that program' — so this is a rate-of-return objection, not an affordability one.
